back:
It turns out that when using operator>> to extract a string from std::cin, operator>> only returns characters up to the first whitespace it encounters. Any other characters are left inside std::cin, waiting for the next extraction.

Use std::getline() to input text.
front: Why can't we use "std::cin >>" by itself to assign a value to an identifier? What do we use instead?
source_suffix: So when we used operator>> to extract input into variable name, only "John" was extracted, leaving " Doe" inside std::cin. When we then used operator>> to get extract input into variable color, it extracted "Doe" instead of waiting for us to input an color. Then the program ends.Use std::getline() to input textTo read a full line of input into a string, you’re better off using the std::getline() function instead. std::getline() requires two arguments: the first is std::cin, and the second is you
